topic: Default and Static Methods in Interfaces

questions.question: What are default methods in Java 8 interfaces?
questions.title: Default Methods in Java 8 Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: A default method is an instance method with a body declared in an interface using `default`. Implementing classes inherit it unless a class method or a more-specific override wins. Default methods give library authors a compatibility path for adding behavior to an interface, although conflicts and behavioral compatibility still need review.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java 8's backward compatibility solution and how default methods enable interface evolution.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not explaining why default methods were added — missing the Collections API evolution story.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use `Collection.stream()` as the Java 8 example, and note that default methods improve interface-evolution compatibility rather than guaranteeing that every implementation remains behaviorally compatible.

sections.title: Why Default Methods Revolutionized Java Interfaces
sections.content:
A **default method** is an instance method with a body inside an interface, declared with the `default` keyword. An implementing class can inherit it or override it.

Before Java 8, adding an abstract method to a published interface usually forced implementers to add that method. A default body provides a source- and binary-compatibility path for many existing implementations. Java 8 used this mechanism for methods such as `Collection.stream()` and `Iterable.forEach()`.

It is not a promise that every possible change is harmless. New defaults can still create inheritance conflicts or have behavior that a custom implementation should override. `default` means that an implementation is already supplied; it does not mean that Java ignores the method.

sections.title: Default Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Default method|~instance method with a body|uses the default keyword|normally inherited|since Java 8
blue|Why added|~aid interface evolution|many existing types inherit a body|Collection.stream()|compatibility still needs review
emerald|Override rules|~concrete class method wins|more-specific interface wins|unrelated conflict needs override|eligible Iface.super call

sections.title: Default Method in a Payment Interface
When to Add Default Methods
sections.content:
Use a default method when an interface has a **sound general implementation**, often built from its existing operations. `Iterable.forEach`, for example, can traverse the iterator that an implementation already provides.

A default can also help **evolve a published interface** because many existing implementations can inherit the new body. Before doing that, check whether the behavior is valid for every implementation, whether another parent interface already declares the signature, and whether clients depend on different semantics. A default is a compatibility tool, not a guarantee that an API change is harmless.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Promising zero compatibility risk**: a new default can conflict with another inherited method or provide behavior a custom implementation should replace.
- **Naming the wrong JDK interface**: Java 8 added `forEach` to `Iterable`; `stream` and `removeIf` are on `Collection`.
- **Thinking default means optional abstract method**: it means the interface already supplies an implementation, subject to normal inheritance and conflict rules.
- **Hiding a service workflow in an interface**: dependency-heavy business orchestration often belongs in a service rather than a default method.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Compatibility tool**: default bodies let many existing implementations keep working when an interface grows
- **Syntax**: `default` appears before the return type and the method has a body
- **Override rules**: class methods and more-specific interface methods take precedence
- **Java 8 examples**: `Collection.stream()` and `removeIf()`, plus `Iterable.forEach()`
- **Conflict boundary**: unrelated equally specific defaults require an explicit override

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A default method is an instance method with a body in an interface. It lets an implementing class inherit working behavior or override it. Java 8 used this as a compatibility tool when adding APIs such as `Collection.stream()` and `Iterable.forEach()`. Adding an abstract method would have required existing implementers to supply it, while a default body gives them an implementation. The boundary is important: a new default can still conflict with another inherited default or be unsuitable for a custom implementation. Java resolves a concrete class method first, then a more-specific interface method; unrelated defaults may require an explicit override.

questions.question: What are static methods in Java 8 interfaces?
questions.title: Static Methods in Java 8 Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: Java 8 allows interfaces to have static methods with implementations. They belong to the interface itself, not implementing classes — they cannot be overridden and are called as InterfaceName.methodName(). They serve as utility or factory methods related to the interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of all Java 8 interface enhancements, not just default methods.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking static interface methods can be called on instances or inherited by implementing classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the Comparator.comparing() example — a widely-used static factory method in an interface.

sections.title: Static Methods as Interface Utilities
sections.content:
A **static method** in an interface is a utility or factory method that belongs to the interface type itself, not to any object that implements it. You call it on the interface name, like `Comparator.comparing()`, and an implementing class does not inherit or override it.

Before Java 8, a helper closely tied to an interface often lived in a separate utility class, such as `Collections`. Static interface methods allow related creation or helper logic to sit next to the contract.

They are useful for two jobs:

- **Factory methods** that return an implementation, such as `Comparator.comparing()` in Java 8.
- **Utility methods** related to the interface that need no instance state.

Java 9 later added factories such as `List.of()`, so it should not be presented as a Java 8 example. The key Java 8 rule is to call the method through the declaring interface, for example `Comparator.comparing(Person::name)`, not through a Comparator instance or an implementing class.

sections.title: Static Interface Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Static method|~utility on the interface itself|called as Interface.method()|not inherited|available since Java 8
blue|Java 8 example|~Comparator.comparing()|factory for a Comparator|keeps creation logic with the contract|List.of() came in Java 9
emerald|Rules|~not overridden by implementers|no instance `this`|call on declaring interface|not inherited

sections.title: Static Factory Methods in Repository Interface
When to Use Static Interface Methods
sections.content:
Use static interface methods for **factory methods** that create implementations of the interface — like `Comparator.comparing()` which builds a Comparator from a function. They're perfect for **utility operations** that work with the interface type but don't need instance state — like validation helpers or common transformations.

Use them when you'd otherwise create a separate utility class just to hold one or two related methods. In REST APIs, I've seen `ResponseHandler.success()` and `ResponseHandler.error()` as static factory methods that create response objects.

Use them for **constants or builders** related to the interface — `PaymentMethod.supportedTypes()` returning a list of valid payment types. The rule is: if the method logically belongs with the interface and doesn't need an instance, make it static in the interface rather than creating a separate utility class.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trying to call a static interface method on an instance**: call `Comparator.comparing(...)` through the declaring interface, not through a Comparator object.
- **Thinking it is inherited**: if class `C` implements interface `I` with static method `m`, `C.m()` is not that inherited method; call `I.m()`.
- **Using a later API as a Java 8 example**: `List.of()` is a static interface method, but it was introduced in Java 9. `Comparator.comparing()` is a Java 8 example.
- **Turning an interface into an unrelated utility bucket**: keep only helpers that belong to that contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Called on interface name**: Use `InterfaceName.methodName()`, never on instances or implementing classes
- **Not inherited**: Implementing classes do not inherit static interface methods — they belong only to the interface
- **Cannot be overridden**: Unlike default methods, static methods cannot be overridden by implementing classes
- **Factory pattern**: Commonly used for factory methods like `Comparator.comparing()` that create instances
- **Utility methods**: Perfect for validation, transformation, or helper methods related to the interface

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Static methods in interfaces are helper methods that belong to the interface itself, not to any class that implements it. You call them using the interface name, like Comparator dot comparing. They can't be overridden and aren't inherited by implementing classes. The main use case is factory methods — methods that create instances of the interface. The best example everyone uses is Comparator dot comparing. If you want to sort a list of users by name, you'd write users dot sort with Comparator dot comparing and pass a lambda. That comparing method is a static method in the Comparator interface that builds a Comparator for you. Before Java 8, you'd need a separate utility class for this, maybe ComparatorUtils or something. Now it lives right in the interface where it belongs. I've used this pattern when building a repository interface — we added static factory methods like UserRepository dot createInMemory and UserRepository dot createWithCache, so client code can easily get the right implementation. The key difference from default methods is that static methods are called on the interface name, not on instances, and they can't be overridden. They're just convenient utilities that live with the interface.

questions.question: What happens when a class inherits two default methods with the same signature from two interfaces?
questions.title: Diamond Problem with Default Methods
questions.direct_answer: If the two defaults come from unrelated interfaces, the implementing class gets a compile-time conflict and must override the method. A concrete class method wins over an interface default, and a more specific subinterface default wins over its parent. In an explicit override, the class may call a direct superinterface default with `InterfaceName.super.methodName()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the diamond problem with default methods and Java's conflict resolution rules.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying every same-signature pair is ambiguous and missing Java's class-wins and more-specific-interface rules.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State all three resolution rules, then demonstrate `InterfaceName.super.method()` for two unrelated direct superinterfaces.

sections.title: The Diamond Problem and Explicit Resolution
sections.content:
A compile-time **diamond conflict** appears when a class would inherit same-signature defaults from two **unrelated** interfaces. Java does not choose by the order in the `implements` list, so the class must override the method.

There are two important cases where Java already has a winner:

- A concrete method inherited from a class wins over an interface default.
- If one interface extends the other, the more specific subinterface default wins.

For two unrelated direct superinterfaces, the overriding class can delegate to one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`, call both deliberately, or supply a new implementation. `InterfaceName.super` must name an eligible direct superinterface; it is not general syntax for reaching any ancestor.

The practical rule is therefore not ‘same signature always fails.’ It is ‘class first, then the most specific interface, otherwise override an unresolved unrelated-default conflict.’

sections.title: The Default-Method Diamond
sections.content:
amber|Conflict|~two interfaces, same default|compiler error|you must resolve it|ambiguity by design
blue|Resolve|~override in your class|call A.super.method()|or B.super.method()|or a fresh body
emerald|Precedence|~class > interface|subtype iface > supertype|explicit super wins|never a silent pick

sections.title: Resolving Conflicting Default Methods
When Conflicts Occur and How to Handle Them
sections.content:
Check the type hierarchy before calling the situation a conflict. If `DetailedLoggable` extends `Loggable` and overrides its default, a class implementing both inherits the more specific `DetailedLoggable` version. If a superclass already has a concrete `record()` method, that class method wins.

An explicit override is required only when unrelated defaults remain. Inside it, use `Auditable.super.record()` or `Loggable.super.record()` to choose a direct superinterface, call both only when both effects are genuinely part of the contract, or write a new implementation. The decision should follow behavior, not merely silence the compiler.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying every pair is ambiguous**: a class method wins, and a more specific subinterface default wins. Only unrelated surviving defaults require an override.
- **Choosing by declaration order**: the order of interfaces in the `implements` clause does not resolve unrelated defaults.
- **Using the wrong `super` form**: inside the override, call an eligible direct superinterface with `Notifier.super.send()`, not plain `super.send()`.
- **Calling both defaults automatically**: combining two effects may duplicate work; choose behavior from the class contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Class wins** — an inherited concrete class method takes priority over an interface default
- **More specific interface wins** — a subinterface override takes priority over its parent default
- **Unrelated defaults conflict** — the implementing class must override when neither interface is more specific
- **Qualified super call** — an override can call an eligible direct superinterface with `InterfaceName.super.method()`
- **No declaration-order rule** — reordering the `implements` list changes nothing

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When a class would inherit the same default signature from two unrelated interfaces, Java reports a compile-time conflict and the class must override the method. In that override it can choose a direct superinterface with `Notifier.super.send()`, deliberately call both, or provide a new body.

There are two precedence rules to state first. A concrete method from a class wins over an interface default. If one interface is more specific because it extends the other, its default wins. Therefore, the error is not caused by every duplicate signature; it occurs when unrelated defaults remain with no more-specific choice. The order of names in the `implements` clause never decides it.

beats.text: The diamond problem appears when a class would inherit same-signature defaults from unrelated interfaces. With no more-specific winner, Java stops at compile time and makes the class override the method.

Java lets a class implement many interfaces, and any of them can carry default bodies. Two equal claims to the same method would be ambiguous, so the language forces a clear decision instead of a hidden one.

items: A concrete class method wins over an interface default.
A more specific subinterface default wins over its parent.
For unrelated surviving defaults, override the method to clear the error.
Inside it, InterfaceName.super.method calls one parent's body on purpose.
Calling both parents in turn blends their behavior into one.
Or you ignore both and write a fresh body from scratch.

Missing the class-wins and more-specific-interface rules.
Writing plain super.send instead of Notifier.super.send, which won't even compile.

questions.question: What is the difference between default methods in interfaces and abstract methods?
questions.title: Default Methods vs Abstract Methods in Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: An abstract interface method declares a required operation without a body; a concrete implementing class must supply or inherit a compatible implementation. A default method has an interface body that is inherited when no class method, more-specific override, or unresolved default conflict takes precedence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Clear distinction between the two types of interface methods and when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing default methods with abstract methods or thinking default still means must implement.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the design decision: use abstract for mandatory contract, default for optional extensions.

sections.title: Mandatory Contract vs Optional Extensions
sections.content:
An **abstract interface method** declares a signature without a body. A concrete class must have a compatible implementation, either declared itself or inherited from a superclass. A **default method** uses the `default` keyword and includes a body in the interface. An implementing class normally inherits that body and may override it.

For example, `Comparable.compareTo` is abstract because each type defines its ordering. A default method can provide reusable behavior built on abstract operations. Java 8 also used defaults for interface evolution: `Iterable` gained `forEach`, while `Collection` gained `stream`. This preserved compatibility for many existing implementations, subject to normal conflict and behavioral rules.

A default is not merely an optional extra; it can be an important part of the contract. The difference is that the interface already supplies its implementation. If unrelated interfaces contribute the same unresolved default, the class must override to resolve the conflict.

sections.title: Default vs Abstract Methods
sections.content:
amber|Default method|~Has a body|lives in an interface|optional to override|since Java 8
blue|Abstract method|~No body|interface or abstract class|must be implemented|the contract itself
emerald|Together|~mix both in one interface|abstract = required|default = provided|impls fill the gaps

sections.title: Abstract method vs default method together
Abstract vs Default Methods
sections.content:
| Aspect | Abstract interface method | Default method |
|---|---|---|
| Body | none | supplied in the interface |
| Concrete class needs an implementation | yes, declared or inherited | normally inherits the default |
| Keyword | implicitly `public abstract` | explicitly `default` |
| Typical role | operation each type must define | reusable behavior or interface evolution |
| Conflict | missing implementation is an error | unresolved competing defaults are an error |

sections.title: When to Use Each Type
sections.content:
Use an **abstract method** when every concrete implementation needs an operation and the interface cannot provide a sound general body. A payment contract may leave `pay(amount)` abstract because each payment mechanism performs different work.

Use a **default method** when there is a correct implementation based on the rest of the interface, or when evolving an established interface with broadly useful behavior. A default `receipt(amount)` might format shared receipt text while still calling abstract accessors supplied by each implementation.

Before adding a default to a published interface, check inherited-name conflicts and whether the new behavior is valid for every implementation. Default methods improve compatibility; they do not guarantee that an API change has no source or behavioral effect.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing terminology**: Freshers see "default method" and think it means a default abstract method that you still have to implement, mixing up "default" with "must have a default." It's actually a method with a default implementation you inherit.
- **Making everything default**: Some freshers avoid abstract methods entirely and make everything default, thinking it's more flexible. This breaks the contract model — if findById is default with an empty implementation, you've lost the enforcement that repositories must provide lookup.
- **Not leveraging abstract in defaults**: Freshers write default methods that duplicate logic instead of calling the abstract methods. A default findAll should call the abstract findById, not reimplement database access.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Abstract = mandatory**: No implementation, must be provided by all non-abstract implementing classes
- **Default = optional**: Has implementation, inherited automatically, can be overridden if needed
- **Contract vs convenience**: Abstract defines core contract, default adds convenience or extensions
- **Compilation**: Missing abstract method implementation causes compile error, missing default override is fine
- **Design principle**: Use abstract for operations that vary, default for operations that are mostly the same

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An abstract interface method declares a required operation but has no body. A concrete implementing class must declare or inherit a compatible implementation. A default method already has a body in the interface, so the class normally inherits it and may override it. For example, `PaymentProcessor.pay` can be abstract because card and bank implementations perform different work, while a default `formatReceipt` can reuse shared formatting. Java 8 also used default methods to evolve established interfaces: `Iterable` gained `forEach`, and `Collection` gained `stream`. That improved compatibility for existing implementations, although competing inherited defaults and behavior changes still need review.

questions.question: Can abstract classes be replaced by interfaces with default methods after Java 8?
questions.title: Abstract Class vs Interface with Default Methods
questions.direct_answer: No. Default methods let an interface supply behavior, but an interface has no constructor or per-instance fields and cannot declare protected instance helpers. An abstract class can initialize and maintain instance state while sharing class behavior; a class may also extend only one class but implement several interfaces.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what abstract classes can still do that interfaces with default methods cannot.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying interfaces and abstract classes are now equivalent after Java 8.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: List specific features only abstract classes have: constructors, instance fields, protected methods, state management.

sections.title: Interfaces Got Behavior But Not State
sections.content:
Default methods did **not** turn interfaces into abstract classes. An interface can supply behavior but has no constructor or per-instance fields. Its fields are implicitly `public static final`; even if such a field refers to a mutable object, that object is shared class-level state rather than state stored separately in each implementation.

An **abstract class** can declare instance fields, initialize them in constructors, expose `protected` or package-private helpers, and coordinate state across method calls. A class can extend only one class, while it may implement several interfaces and inherit compatible defaults from them.

Use an abstract class when shared instance state, construction rules, or class-oriented template behavior is central. Use an interface when the main need is a contract across potentially unrelated types. Many designs use both: an interface for the public capability and an optional abstract base class for shared implementation.

sections.title: Interface vs Abstract Class after Java 8
sections.content:
amber|Interface (Java 8+)|~default + static methods|multiple inheritance|no instance state|no constructors
blue|Abstract class|~fields + constructors|protected members|single inheritance|partial state machine
emerald|Verdict|~not fully replaceable|need state -> abstract class|stateless behavior -> interface|often use both

sections.title: Interface cannot hold mutable state
Abstract class keeps state + a constructor
What Abstract Classes Still Offer
sections.content:
| Feature | Abstract class | Interface with defaults |
|---|---|---|
| Per-instance fields | yes | no; interface fields are `public static final` |
| Constructors | yes | no |
| Helper visibility | public, protected, package-private, private | public; private interface methods from Java 9, no protected |
| Class inheritance | a class extends one class | a class may implement several interfaces |
| Typical role | shared state and class implementation | capability contract and reusable stateless behavior |

sections.title: When You Still Need Abstract Classes
sections.content:
Use **abstract classes** when you need **shared state** across methods — like a base `Entity` class with a common `id` field and `createdAt` timestamp that all entities inherit.

Use them for **initialization logic** — if subclasses need constructor parameters validated or resources allocated, abstract class constructors handle this.

Use them for **template method patterns** where a method manages state and calls abstract methods in sequence.

Use abstract classes for **protected methods** that should be visible to subclasses but not to external clients — interfaces can't do protected. In Spring applications, I've used abstract repository base classes that hold the EntityManager field and provide protected helper methods for query building.

Use **interfaces with defaults** when you need **multiple inheritance** of behavior without state, or when you're evolving existing APIs. If you need both, combine them: interface for contract, abstract class for common state and logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking they're now equivalent**: The biggest mistake is saying "we don't need abstract classes anymore" after learning about default methods. Abstract classes still have unique capabilities around state and constructors.
- **Trying to add state to interfaces**: Freshers attempt to declare instance fields in interfaces, not realizing interfaces can only have static final constants.
- **Forgetting about constructors**: When initialization logic is needed, freshers create complex static factory methods in interfaces instead of just using an abstract class with a constructor.
- **Ignoring protected visibility**: Freshers miss that protected methods for controlled inheritance only exist in abstract classes, not interfaces.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Instance fields**: Abstract classes can have mutable state, interfaces can only have static final constants
- **Constructors**: Only abstract classes have constructors for initialization logic and field setup
- **Access control**: Abstract classes support protected methods, interfaces only public or private (Java 9+)
- **State management**: Abstract classes manage and modify state across methods, interfaces are stateless
- **Single vs multiple**: Abstract classes support single inheritance, interfaces support multiple implementation

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: No, they can't fully replace abstract classes, even though default methods made interfaces more powerful. Abstract classes can still do things interfaces can't. The biggest one is instance fields — abstract classes can have mutable state that's shared across methods. Let's say you've got a base Entity class with an id field and a createdAt timestamp. Every subclass inherits those fields. You can't do that with an interface because interfaces can only have static final constants, not instance variables. Second is constructors — abstract classes can have constructors that initialize fields and run setup logic when objects are created. Interfaces have no constructors at all. Third is access control — abstract classes can have protected methods that are visible to subclasses but hidden from external code. Interfaces in Java 8 only have public methods, though Java 9 added private. So when do you use what? Use interfaces with defaults when you need multiple inheritance of behavior and you're working with stateless operations. Use abstract classes when you need shared state, initialization logic, or the template method pattern where a parent method manages state and calls abstract methods. In practice, you often use both — an interface defines the contract, an abstract class provides common state and logic, and concrete classes extend the abstract class while implementing additional interfaces.

questions.question: What are some real examples of default methods added to Java's Collections API in Java 8?
questions.title: Real Default Methods in Java Collections API
questions.direct_answer: Java 8 added `forEach()` to `Iterable`; `removeIf()`, `stream()`, and `parallelStream()` to `Collection`; `replaceAll()` and `sort()` to `List`; and methods such as `computeIfAbsent()` and `merge()` to `Map`. Default implementations allowed existing types to gain these APIs with broad source and binary compatibility, although new default-method conflicts or behavior assumptions can still require attention.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate connects default methods to actual APIs they use daily, not just theory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that stream() and forEach() are default methods added in Java 8.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how removeIf() and replaceAll() replace verbose iterator-based loops with cleaner code.

sections.title: How Java 8 Evolved the Collections Interfaces
sections.content:
Java 8 added many **default methods** across the Collections Framework so established interfaces could gain lambda- and stream-friendly operations without forcing every implementation to declare each new method.

The declaring interfaces matter. `Iterable` gained `forEach()`. `Collection` gained `removeIf()`, `stream()`, and `parallelStream()`. `List` gained `sort()` and `replaceAll()`. `Map`, which is not a subtype of `Collection`, gained methods including `getOrDefault()`, `putIfAbsent()`, `computeIfAbsent()`, `merge()`, `forEach()`, and `replaceAll()`.

Examples:

- **`stream()`** creates a stream pipeline from a collection.
- **`forEach()`** applies an action during iteration.
- **`removeIf()`** asks a modifiable collection to remove matching elements; an unsupported removal can still throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- **`Map.computeIfAbsent()`** computes a mapping when the key has no value, subject to that Map implementation's concurrency rules.

Default methods preserve broad source and binary compatibility, which made this interface evolution practical. They do not promise that every old custom implementation has ideal semantics, supports mutation, or can never encounter a new inherited-default conflict.

sections.content:

blue|List|~replaceAll(operator)|sort(comparator)|in-place updates|no new list created
emerald|Map|~getOrDefault / putIfAbsent|computeIfAbsent / merge|forEach((k,v) -> ...)|replaceAll

sections.title: Using Collection Default Methods
Real-World Usage of Collection Default Methods
sections.content:
Use **stream()** when a filter, transformation, grouping, or reduction reads naturally as a pipeline. A loop may still be clearer for indexed control, mutation, or several early exits.

Use **forEach()** for a final action such as printing each element, not as a default replacement for every loop. Use **removeIf()** when the collection supports removal and a predicate clearly states which elements to delete.

Use **List.sort()** and **List.replaceAll()** when an in-place list change is intended. Use **Map.computeIfAbsent()** for a value derived from a missing key, while checking the chosen Map's rules about nulls, recursion, and atomicity. Use **Map.merge()** for concise updates such as word counts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Naming the wrong declaring interface**: `forEach()` was added to `Iterable`, while `stream()` and `removeIf()` are on `Collection`; `Map` is a separate branch.
- **Assuming all collections are mutable**: `removeIf()`, `sort()`, and `replaceAll()` can throw `UnsupportedOperationException` when the implementation does not support the change.
- **Assuming every `computeIfAbsent()` is an atomic cache loader**: concurrency and mapping-function guarantees depend on the Map implementation; read its contract.
- **Using `forEach()` for external accumulation**: a collector or ordinary loop often makes ownership and concurrency clearer.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **stream() and parallelStream()**: Enable functional data processing pipelines on any Collection
- **forEach()**: Applies a lambda to each element, replacing traditional for-each loops
- **removeIf()**: Removes elements matching a predicate, cleaner than iterator-based removal
- **List.sort()**: Sorts the list in-place using a Comparator, replacing Collections.sort()
- **List.replaceAll()**: Transforms each element in-place using a UnaryOperator

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Java 8 added lambda- and stream-friendly defaults across several Collections Framework interfaces. `Iterable` gained `forEach`. `Collection` gained `removeIf`, `stream`, and `parallelStream`. `List` gained `sort` and `replaceAll`. `Map`, which is separate from `Collection`, gained methods such as `getOrDefault`, `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`, `forEach`, and `replaceAll`. The declaring interface matters because the available operations and their contracts come from that interface and its implementation. These defaults let many existing implementations inherit useful behavior instead of immediately declaring every new method. They provide broad compatibility, not a promise of zero impact: removal may be unsupported, Map methods follow the chosen implementation's null and concurrency rules, and inherited defaults can conflict. For example, `computeIfAbsent` is useful when a missing key should derive a value, but its atomicity and recursion rules depend on the Map implementation.

speakable_v2.hook: Java 8 added `stream`, `removeIf`, `sort`, and several Map helpers through default methods. The methods live on different interfaces in the Collections Framework.

beats.text: Default bodies let established interfaces add useful operations without requiring every implementation to declare each one immediately. Existing types inherited the applicable methods, subject to normal mutability and conflict rules.
The Collections API was twenty years old and everywhere. Java wanted streams and lambdas on it. Default methods let the team bolt on new behavior, so they didn't force a single rewrite.

items: Collection got stream and parallelStream, the doorway into the Stream API.
Iterable got forEach, so a lambda runs on each element with no loop.
Collection got removeIf, which deletes matches without an iterator.
List got sort and replaceAll, both updating the list in place.

beats.text: Say you hold a list of orders. orders.forEach prints each one. orders.removeIf drops the shipped ones, and orders.stream sums the prices. Here's the non-obvious part. Map joined in too with getOrDefault and computeIfAbsent, which kill a heap of null checks.

items: Not realizing stream and forEach are default methods, then freezing when an interviewer asks how they were added.
Using forEach to mutate an outside list, which throws away the clean functional style.

speakable_v2.cap: So remember where they live: `forEach` on Iterable, stream and removeIf on Collection, sort and replaceAll on List, and compute or merge helpers on Map.
